blocks.prompt: The Eggs in the River Bank
blocks.text: Almost every mammal has babies that are born alive. The platypus does not. The mother platypus digs a long burrow in the river bank. She lays two small eggs, softer than a bird's egg. She curls around them to keep them warm. In about ten days the babies hatch. They are pink and blind and smaller than your thumb. The mother has no way to feed them milk from a teat. Her milk leaks out through her skin instead. The babies lap it up from her fur.

3.title: The Animal Nobody Believed In
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Say it PLAT-uh-puss

blocks.prompt: Hunting Blind
blocks.text: A platypus hunts in muddy water where almost nothing can be seen. So it does something strange. Just before it dives, it shuts its eyes. It shuts its ears. It shuts its nostrils too. For the whole dive, the platypus is blind and deaf, and it does not care. The trick is the bill. A platypus bill is not hard like a duck's beak. It is soft and rubbery, and it is packed with about a hundred thousand tiny sensors. Most of those sensors feel pressure, the way your fingertip feels a nudge. About forty thousand of them do something no other mammal in the world can do well. They pick up electricity. Every time a shrimp flicks its tail, its muscles give off a faint spark of electricity. The water carries that spark. The platypus sweeps its bill from side to side, catches the signal, and turns straight toward it. It finds its dinner in the dark without ever opening its eyes.

answers: its eyes, its ears, and its nostrils
it is soft and rubbery instead of hard
pressure, and electricity from a shrimp's muscles
(inference: eyes are no use in muddy water, so the bill tells it more than seeing would)

4.title: The Animal Nobody Believed In
4.subtitle: A reading and history of science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Skin That Looked Like a Lie
blocks.text: In 1799 a package arrived in London from the new British colony in Australia. Inside was the dried skin of an animal that could not exist. It had the flat bill of a duck stitched, apparently, onto the furred body of a mole. It had webbed feet, and a tail like a beaver's paddle. George Shaw, a naturalist at the British Museum, was not fooled. Or rather, he expected to prove he was not fooled. Taxidermists in Asia were known to sew monkey bodies onto fish tails and sell them as mermaids, so Shaw took a pair of scissors to the bill and hunted for the stitches. He found none. The bill had grown there. He published a careful description and admitted, in print, that he could not shake the suspicion of trickery. The animal was worse than Shaw imagined. Over the following decades, reports came back from Australia claiming that this furred, warm-blooded creature laid eggs. European scientists argued about it for nearly ninety years. Mammals had fur and milk and live young. Birds and reptiles laid eggs. The categories were tidy, and the platypus sat in the wrong one. It was not settled until 1884, when William Caldwell found a platypus with an egg and sent a short telegram to a meeting of scientists in Montreal. Today we know the platypus is a monotreme, a mammal that lays eggs. There are only five monotreme species left on Earth: the platypus and four kinds of echidna. They are not a failed experiment. They are the oldest branch of the mammal family still living.

5.title: The Animal Nobody Believed In
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ornithorhynchus anatinus
Bill: about 40,000 electric sensors, about 60,000 pressure sensors
Males have a venom spur on each hind ankle
No teeth: it grinds its food with gravel
Ten sex chromosomes, not two
The monotreme line split off over 160 million years ago

blocks.prompt: A Mammal Assembled From Spare Parts
blocks.text: People like to describe the platypus as an animal built from leftover parts: a duck's bill, an otter's feet, a beaver's tail, all stapled onto something like a mole. It is a good joke and a bad description. Nothing about the platypus is borrowed. Every piece of it evolved on its own, in Australian rivers, for a reason. Start with the bill, which is nothing like a duck's. A duck's beak is hard keratin. The platypus bill is soft, flexible skin stretched over bone, and it works as a sense organ rather than a tool. Around sixty thousand receptors in it detect pressure. Around forty thousand more detect electricity, and researchers think the platypus uses both together: the electric signal from a shrimp's twitching muscle arrives at the bill a fraction of a second before the pressure wave from the same movement does. The size of that gap tells the platypus how far away the shrimp is. It is hunting by a kind of biological arithmetic, in total darkness, with its eyes squeezed shut. Then there is the spur. On the inside of each hind ankle, a male platypus carries a hollow, curved spike connected to a venom gland. The venom will not kill a person, which is the only reassuring thing about it. Victims describe pain so severe that morphine does not touch it, and swelling that can last for months. The gland swells during breeding season and shrinks afterward, which tells us what the venom is for. It is not aimed at predators or at prey. It is aimed at other males. The feeding is stranger still. An adult platypus has no teeth at all. It scoops up prey along with a mouthful of gravel, stores the lot in its cheek pouches, surfaces, and grinds the meal against horny pads using the grit as sandpaper. The oddest fact is the one you cannot see. Most mammals, including you, carry two sex chromosomes. The platypus carries ten, and they link together in a chain during reproduction. Its genome, read in full in 2008, contains genes that look reptilian sitting next to genes that look thoroughly mammalian. None of this makes the platypus primitive. It makes it old. The monotreme line split from the rest of the mammals more than one hundred and sixty million years ago and has been quietly refining itself in Australian water ever since.

6.title: The Animal Nobody Believed In
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ornithorhynchus anatinus: bird-snout, duck-like
Monotreme: lays eggs, makes milk, has fur
Bill: about 40,000 electroreceptors, about 60,000 push rods
Ten sex chromosomes that link in a chain
Genome sequenced in 2008: reptile and mammal genes side by side
Its fur glows blue-green under UV light, reported in 2020
IUCN status: Near Threatened

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Broke the Categories
blocks.text: For most of the nineteenth century, the platypus was a scandal. The trouble began in 1799, when a dried skin reached London from the penal colony at New South Wales. George Shaw, describing it for the British Museum, could not persuade himself it was real. Asian taxidermists had a known trade in mermaids assembled from monkeys and fish, and this thing looked like a better version of the same fraud: a duck's bill on a mole's body, with webbed feet and a flat, furred paddle for a tail. Shaw took scissors to the bill and searched for stitching. There was none. He published anyway, and confessed in the same breath that he could not shake his doubts. The scandal deepened when colonists reported that the animal laid eggs. This was not a curiosity. It was a threat. European naturalists had spent a century sorting life into clean containers: mammals have fur, produce milk, and bear live young; birds and reptiles lay eggs. A furred, milk-producing egg-layer did not belong in any container, and rather than widen the containers, many scientists simply refused to believe the reports. The argument ran for eighty-five years. It ended in 1884, when William Caldwell, working in Queensland, found a platypus with an egg and sent a telegram to a scientific meeting in Montreal, confirming what Aboriginal Australians had known for thousands of years and colonists had been saying for decades. What the platypus exposed was not a gap in nature. It was a gap in the filing system. Nature never agreed to the categories; people invented them, working mostly from the animals of Europe, and then mistook their own invention for a law. The platypus was never a contradiction. It was simply older than the rule it appeared to break. The monotreme lineage split from the rest of the mammals more than one hundred and sixty million years ago, long before live birth became the standard, and it kept the egg because the egg kept working. Look closely and the platypus stops looking like a mixture at all. The bill is not a duck's beak; a duck's beak is hard keratin, while the platypus bill is soft skin over bone, carrying roughly forty thousand electroreceptors and sixty thousand pressure receptors. Diving with its eyes, ears, and nostrils clamped shut, the animal reads the faint electrical twitch of a shrimp's muscle and, researchers believe, judges distance from the delay between that electric signal and the slower pressure wave behind it. The male's ankle spur delivers a venom that will not kill a human but produces pain that morphine reportedly cannot reach. The gland feeding it swells in breeding season, which suggests the weapon is for settling disputes with rival males, not for defense. Each of these is a specialist solution to a specific Australian problem. None of them is borrowed. The modern chapter is quieter and worse. The platypus is not a scandal now; it is a species in slow retreat. It needs permanent freshwater, stable banks to burrow into, and enough shrimp and insect larvae to fuel a metabolism that burns through roughly a fifth of its body weight in food each night. Dams fragment its rivers, drought dries them, and the animal cannot cross dry country to find better water. The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened, and long stretches of river that carried platypuses within living memory now carry none. The nineteenth century argued about whether the platypus could possibly exist. That question is settled. The one left is whether we intend to let it keep existing, and unlike the first, this one is not about evidence. It is about choice.
